blocks.text: **The task.** Decide whether a string reads the same forwards and backwards, considering only letters and digits, and ignoring case.

blocks.code:
"A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"   ->  true
"race a car"                       ->  false

blocks.text: The tempting solution is to clean the string, reverse the copy, and compare. Correct, but it builds two extra strings — O(N) space to answer a yes/no question.

Better to observe what a palindrome *means*: the first useful character matches the last, the second matches the second-to-last, and so on. That is a pairing across the centre — the direct two pointer shape.
Walk from both ends. When a pointer lands on punctuation or a space, skip it. When both are on real characters, compare them — any mismatch means we are done.
The inner skip loops repeat `left < right` in their own conditions. Without it, a string of nothing but punctuation would run a pointer straight past the end of the string.
Note also that we return `false` the instant a mismatch appears. A palindrome must match everywhere, so one failure settles it — there is no reason to keep looking.
**Time: O(N)** — each pointer only ever moves inward, so between them they cover the string once. The nested loops look suspicious but never rescan.
**Space: O(1)** — no cleaned copy, no reversed string.
